concepts.title: Pancreatic insulin pulse
concepts.shortExplanation: After a meal, beta cells increase insulin release so peripheral tissues can clear glucose.
misconceptions: Insulin is always low in Type 2 diabetes from the start.
Pancreas output is unrelated to meal size.
hints: Compare meal size with insulin curve height.
Look for timing: insulin rise follows glucose rise.
Check whether insulin rise is sufficient for uptake.
challenges: Increase meal size and keep post-meal peak under control by adjusting activity.
Find a setting where insulin rises but glucose still normalizes quickly.
concepts.glossaryDefinition: Beta-cell insulin pulse is the short-term rise in insulin secretion after glucose intake.

concepts.title: Hepatic output suppression
concepts.shortExplanation: In normal regulation, insulin suppresses excess hepatic glucose output after meals.
misconceptions: Liver output turns off completely after eating.
Hepatic output only matters at night.
hints: Track fasting glucose alongside hepatic output index.
Notice if output stays elevated despite insulin.
Relate hepatic output to pre-meal glucose levels.
challenges: Find settings where fasting glucose stays near baseline while meal response remains stable.

concepts.title: Muscle GLUT4 uptake
concepts.shortExplanation: Muscle uptake increases via GLUT4 translocation, especially when activity is higher.
misconceptions: Activity does not change glucose clearance.
GLUT4 only matters in adipose tissue.
hints: Increase activity and inspect peripheral uptake index.
Look for post-meal peak reduction when uptake rises.
Compare with low-activity state.
challenges: Use activity changes to improve glucose recovery without increasing inflammation.

concepts.title: Adipose metabolic buffering
concepts.shortExplanation: Adipose tissue influences insulin sensitivity through lipid flux and inflammatory signaling.
misconceptions: Adipose tissue is only passive storage.
FFA signals do not affect insulin pathways.
hints: Toggle high FFA and observe sensitivity drop.
Watch both insulin effectiveness and hepatic output.
Link inflammation increase to glucose shift.
challenges: Identify which stressor makes sensitivity fall fastest in your settings.

concepts.title: Glucose-insulin curve coupling
concepts.shortExplanation: Healthy regulation shows coordinated curves: insulin rises and glucose returns toward baseline.
misconceptions: Only glucose curve matters for physiology.
Insulin and glucose curves are independent.
hints: Compare peak timing between curves.
Check if baseline recovery is delayed.
Use both curves to infer control quality.
challenges: Create a scenario with modest peak and clean baseline return within the timeline.

concepts.title: Insulin receptor weakening
concepts.shortExplanation: Inflammation and lipid stress weaken receptor signaling, lowering response to insulin.
misconceptions: Resistance means no insulin is present.
Receptor changes do not affect hepatic output.
hints: Enable inflammation and compare insulin effectiveness.
Notice whether glucose rises despite insulin level.
Check downstream uptake index.
challenges: Build a state where insulin is moderate but glucose remains high due to poor signaling.

concepts.title: Reduced GLUT4 translocation
concepts.shortExplanation: When signaling weakens, less GLUT4 reaches the membrane and uptake declines.
misconceptions: GLUT4 changes only affect fasting glucose.
GLUT4 is unrelated to insulin sensitivity.
hints: Track peripheral uptake after adding stressors.
Compare post-meal peaks with and without high FFA.
Observe uptake before and after activity increase.
challenges: Find the minimum activity needed to partially compensate for a GLUT4-limited state.

concepts.title: Increased hepatic output in resistance
concepts.shortExplanation: Insulin resistance can raise hepatic output, pushing fasting glucose upward.
misconceptions: High fasting glucose must come only from meals.
Liver output is unaffected by sensitivity.
hints: Compare fasting glucose across sensitivity values.
Observe hepatic index when inflammation is high.
Link fasting shift to liver output trend.
challenges: Create a high-fasting scenario without changing meal size.

concepts.title: FFA-inflammation feedback loop
concepts.shortExplanation: FFA load and inflammatory tone can reinforce resistance and impair glucose control.
misconceptions: FFA load only changes lipid markers.
Inflammation does not alter insulin pathways.
hints: Toggle both high FFA and inflammation together.
Watch insulin effectiveness and glucose-level jump.
Then remove one stressor and compare.
challenges: Identify which single stressor contributes more in your current section setup.

concepts.title: Early compensatory hyperinsulinemia
concepts.shortExplanation: Early resistance often shows higher insulin output before overt beta-cell decline.
misconceptions: Resistance always starts with low insulin.
Higher insulin means sensitivity is normal.
hints: Watch insulin curve first, then glucose curve.
Look for cases where insulin rises but glucose still elevated.
Compare with later-stage beta failure states.
challenges: Generate a state with high insulin but still impaired glucose clearance.

concepts.title: Beta-cell compensation phase
concepts.shortExplanation: Beta cells increase secretion to offset resistance during earlier progression.
misconceptions: Compensation means disease is absent.
Compensation can continue indefinitely without stress.
hints: At lower stage values, inspect insulin output relative to glucose.
Look for temporary maintenance of fasting values.
Track when this pattern breaks.
challenges: Find the stage point where compensation starts to fail visibly.

concepts.title: Glucotoxic stress on beta cells
concepts.shortExplanation: Sustained high glucose contributes to beta-cell stress and reduced function.
misconceptions: Glucotoxicity appears only in severe late disease.
Beta-cell function is unaffected by sustained peaks.
hints: Increase stage and observe fasting trend.
Inspect post-meal peaks over repeated high-load settings.
Relate persistent peaks to lower beta function.
challenges: Create prolonged high-peak conditions and describe beta function drift.

concepts.title: Lipotoxic stress
concepts.shortExplanation: Excess lipid exposure can worsen beta-cell performance and insulin signaling.
misconceptions: Lipid stress only affects cardiovascular outcomes.
FFA does not influence beta-cell decline.
hints: Combine high FFA with progression stage increase.
Watch insulin and glucose divergence.
Compare to low-FFA baseline.
challenges: Demonstrate a scenario where FFA load accelerates failure trajectory.

concepts.title: Fasting glucose crossover
concepts.shortExplanation: As compensation fails, fasting glucose rises and may cross diabetic thresholds.
misconceptions: Only post-meal glucose changes during progression.
Fasting glucose remains stable until very late.
hints: Adjust stage and monitor fasting values first.
Then inspect post-meal peak.
Note which crosses threshold earlier in your run.
challenges: Find the earliest stage where fasting exceeds 126 mg/dL.

concepts.title: Postprandial spike amplification
concepts.shortExplanation: Reduced beta reserve magnifies post-meal spikes and delays return to baseline.
misconceptions: Post-meal spikes are only meal-size effects.
Insulin reserve does not alter peak recovery time.
hints: Keep meal size fixed and move stage slider.
Compare peak height and late curve tail.
Check insulin curve flattening.
challenges: Maintain meal size and show how stage alone changes post-meal behavior.

concepts.title: Cardiometabolic risk trajectory
concepts.shortExplanation: Chronic dysglycemia and inflammation increase cardiovascular risk burden over time.
misconceptions: Heart risk only changes with blood pressure, not glycemia.
Short spikes never matter for vascular stress.
hints: Raise chronic exposure and inspect heart bar.
Compare with lower inflammation states.
Link trend to chronic load.
challenges: Increase exposure until heart risk exceeds 60 while keeping other sliders stable.

concepts.title: Kidney vulnerability
concepts.shortExplanation: Kidney risk rises with chronic glycemic stress and sustained metabolic burden.
misconceptions: Kidney risk follows only short-term meal peaks.
Kidney exposure is unrelated to fasting shifts.
hints: Track kidney risk while moving exposure.
Observe effect of hepatic output on kidney trend.
Compare kidney vs heart slope.
challenges: Find conditions where kidney risk climbs faster than heart risk.

concepts.title: Retinal microvascular stress
concepts.shortExplanation: Retinal risk can rise with sustained hyperglycemia and microvascular stress.
misconceptions: Eye risk appears only after severe symptoms.
Retinal risk is independent of chronic glucose load.
hints: Increase chronic exposure and inspect eye risk.
Compare eye and nerve progression.
Note role of inflammation in risk bars.
challenges: Produce a state where eye risk enters warning range while heart remains lower.

concepts.title: Neuropathy tendency
concepts.shortExplanation: Nerve risk reflects cumulative metabolic and vascular stress patterns.
misconceptions: Nerve risk is unrelated to glycemic control.
Neuropathy progression is immediate and binary.
hints: Watch nerve bar over exposure increases.
Compare with eye and kidney risk patterns.
Look for trend rather than one-point value.
challenges: Create a scenario where nerve risk exceeds 70 and explain which controls drove it.

concepts.title: Neurovascular risk
concepts.shortExplanation: Neurovascular risk can increase with persistent metabolic stress and inflammation.
misconceptions: Brain risk is completely independent of glucose patterns.
Only acute events matter, not cumulative load.
hints: Track brain risk as exposure rises.
Inspect interaction with inflammation changes.
Compare brain and heart trajectories.
challenges: Increase brain risk while minimizing additional meal-size changes.

concepts.title: Insulin resistance
concepts.shortExplanation: Cells respond less effectively to insulin signaling.
misconceptions: Resistance means no insulin exists.
Resistance has no effect on liver output.
hints: Compare insulin effectiveness with glucose level.
Observe receptor-to-GLUT4 pathway changes.
challenges: Use stressors to push insulin effectiveness below 50% and describe the result.
concepts.glossaryDefinition: Reduced biological response to insulin, requiring higher levels for similar glucose control.

concepts.title: GLUT4
concepts.shortExplanation: GLUT4 transporters increase glucose entry into muscle and adipose cells.
misconceptions: GLUT4 does not depend on insulin signaling.
GLUT4 only affects fasting state.
hints: Inspect uptake index under resistance.
Check post-meal peak changes.
challenges: Find a setup that improves GLUT4-mediated uptake via activity.
concepts.glossaryDefinition: Insulin-responsive glucose transporter that translocates to the cell membrane.

concepts.title: Hepatic glucose output
concepts.shortExplanation: Glucose released by liver, especially relevant in fasting state.
misconceptions: Hepatic output is meal-only.
Output cannot be altered by insulin effectiveness.
hints: Watch fasting glucose alongside hepatic index.
Compare low vs high inflammation.
challenges: Lower hepatic output index using any two control changes.
concepts.glossaryDefinition: Liver-derived glucose production that contributes to circulating glucose levels.

concepts.title: Beta-cell compensation
concepts.shortExplanation: Temporary increase in insulin secretion to offset resistance.
misconceptions: Compensation means disease reversal.
Compensation does not have limits.
hints: Check early stage insulin behavior.
Watch transition toward failure.
challenges: Identify stage where compensation is no longer sufficient.
concepts.glossaryDefinition: Early adaptive increase in insulin output in response to resistance.

concepts.title: Glucotoxicity
concepts.shortExplanation: Cell dysfunction caused by chronic high glucose exposure.
misconceptions: Only severe immediate spikes cause toxicity.
Beta-cell function is unaffected by chronic exposure.
hints: Increase stage and monitor fasting values.
Compare repeated high-peak scenarios.
challenges: Demonstrate how persistent peaks can worsen baseline trends.
concepts.glossaryDefinition: Adverse cellular effects from prolonged hyperglycemia.

concepts.title: Lipotoxicity
concepts.shortExplanation: Cell stress from chronic excess lipid signaling and free fatty acids.
misconceptions: Lipids only affect weight, not signaling.
FFA load has no beta-cell impact.
hints: Toggle high FFA and inspect curve shifts.
Pair high FFA with stage progression.
challenges: Show a scenario where FFA increases both resistance and progression burden.
concepts.glossaryDefinition: Cellular dysfunction induced by excess lipid and free fatty acid exposure.

concepts.title: Postprandial glucose
concepts.shortExplanation: Glucose level after eating, often used to assess meal response.
misconceptions: Postprandial changes are not clinically relevant.
Only fasting glucose indicates control.
hints: Use meal size slider and compare peak.
Track recovery slope after the peak.
challenges: Reduce post-meal peak below 180 with control adjustments.
concepts.glossaryDefinition: Blood glucose concentration measured after a meal.

concepts.title: Fasting glucose
concepts.shortExplanation: Baseline glucose after a fasting interval, strongly linked to hepatic output.
misconceptions: Fasting glucose depends only on last meal.
Liver output has no fasting influence.
hints: Adjust inflammation and sensitivity.
Watch hepatic output and fasting together.
challenges: Create a setting where fasting glucose crosses 126 without changing meal size.
concepts.glossaryDefinition: Baseline blood glucose level measured after fasting.

concepts.title: Peripheral uptake
concepts.shortExplanation: Glucose clearance into peripheral tissues, especially skeletal muscle.
misconceptions: Peripheral uptake does not affect post-meal peak.
Uptake cannot improve with activity.
hints: Increase activity and inspect uptake index.
Compare post-meal peak reduction.
challenges: Raise uptake index above 0.6 while keeping inflammation moderate.
concepts.glossaryDefinition: Transfer of blood glucose into peripheral tissues for utilization or storage.

concepts.title: Chronic hyperglycemia exposure
concepts.shortExplanation: Accumulated glycemic burden over time that drives systemic risk progression.
misconceptions: Only current glucose matters for risk.
Complication risk cannot accumulate gradually.
hints: Increase exposure slider and observe risk bars.
Compare organ-specific sensitivity.
challenges: Raise chronic exposure until two organ risks exceed 60.
concepts.glossaryDefinition: Long-duration glycemic burden associated with progressive organ risk.
